messages.subject: First stub of the autoplot package
messages.subject_clean: First stub of the autoplot package
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

A while ago I asked about best practices for developing packages, with the aim of developing an autoplot package to extend ggplot2's functionality. I got plenty of good suggestions and a first stub of implementation is now there:
	https://github.com/jiho/autoplot
it implements fortify and autoplot methods for Principal Component Analysis, for both stats::prcomp and FactoMineR::PCA.

You can try it with
	library("devtools")
	install_github("autoplot", "jiho")
	library("autoplot")
	example("autoplot.pca")
	?autoplot.pca
	?fortify.pca
What I particularly like with the whole autoplot approach is having most of the plot made for you but still being able to add new mappings on the output. Hopefully that will seduce people other than me ;)

It's my first package and I tried to be as clean as possible while setting up the development environment to use testthat, roxygen2 etc., so that took some time. I would appreciate if the knowledgeable people on this list could have a look at the code and point at my mistakes (in particular, I am very unfamiliar with the whole namespace thing). I added comments with TODOs so that you can see where I am going. Oh, and I am not a native english speaker so do not hesitate to suggest better wording for the documentation!

Thanks in advance to everyone!

PS: By the way, the variables plot in the example suggests that coord_fixed() does not give an exact 1:1 aspect ratio. The unit circle looks slightly stretched horizontally to me. Is that just me?

Jean-Olivier Irisson

Hi Brandon,

Thanks for the feedback.

On 2012-Jul-05, at 23:18 , Brandon Hurr wrote:
>
> I will be trying this in the morning. Thanks for your efforts. I have used ggplot to plot PCA data previously and it does make very nice plots. I've been using pcaMethods from bioconductor. Perhaps I can help make a fortify for that. One issue with PCA in R is a seeming lack of missing data handling and cross validation.

I've more experience with FactoMineR. It replaces missing data with the column's mean, which effectively makes it zero weight. Now if there are quite a few missing points, the people behind FactoMineR also coded the package missMDA which imputes the missing data through iterative PCA. I've tested this and got mixed results depending on the shape of the data of course. But if you have good explanatory power on the PCA + missing data that is well spread-out, it works quite well.

I'm not sure what you mean by cross-validation; split the dataset in bits, and repeat the PCA on various combinations of the bits, to check how robust the results are? I guess the boot package can probably help.

> That and the data you pass to the PCA computation cannot have non numerical columns. Which means you strip it of factors that you then have to cabins back in order to use colors, shapes, and sizes to differentiate groups of data to visualize associations.

Again, FactoMineR lets you use qualitative supplementary variables; those are not used to compute the projection but they can then be projected into the observations space. Essentially, it projects the barycenter of each level of the factor.

But even without this, with the current code in autoplot, if you provide the data together with the model, you can map aesthetics to columns of the original data which where not necessarily used in the PCA:

d <- data.frame(a=runif(10), b=runif(10), c=runif(10), foo=factor(round(runif(10,1, 3))))
pca <- prcomp(d[,-4], scale=T)
library("autoplot")
autoplot(pca, data=d)
autoplot(pca, data=d, mapping=aes(shape=foo))

library("FactoMineR")
pca <- PCA(d, quali.sup=4, graph=F)
autoplot(pca)
autoplot(pca, mapping=aes(shape=foo))

> Also, I never could figure out how to get a biplot scaled correctly and compute the hotellings circle though....

I'm French so I've been raised since childhood to hate biplots ;)
More seriously, I don't know why, there's a cultural bias against biplots here so I did not even try to produce one yet. I seem to recall that Hadley did not like them too. Overall, having two separate plots with two very different scales on the same graphic does not seem like a good idea indeed.

messages.body_plain:
I've been making a score plot function for my own package, based on ggplot2, but it is so specific that I have yet to make it a standalone. I will have a look at your code when time permits...

The hottelling statistics can be computed as: (For a data frame with each PC in a column)

simconf <- function(X, alfa=0.95){

df1 <- ncol(X)

df2 <- nrow(X)

R <- as.data.frame(matrix(0, nrow=df1, ncol=4))

for (i in 1:df1){

m <- mean(X[,i])

int <- sqrt((df1*(df2-1))/(df2-df1)*qf(alfa,df1,df2-df1))*sd(X[,i])

R[i,] <- c(m, int, m-int, m+int)

}

names(R) <- c("Mean", "+/-", "Lower limit", "Upper limit")

row.names(R) <- paste("PC", as.character(1:df1), sep="")

R

}

Sorry for the badly named variables...

I ended up scaling the variables in the biplot based on the Hottelling stats, so that the highest loading was placed ~5 % longer away from the centre than the circle... I don't think there is any best approach...

I have also created some evaluation plots, such as leverage vs. distance to model, which I think are nice to have around

Thanks for the effort - I'm seduced : )

OD = ||xi-P.t’||

Hubert et al 2005 take (median(OD^2/3)+MAD(OD2/3)*z0.975)^3/2 where z0.975 is the 97,5% quantile of the normal distribution as the critical OD

Actually, I think you are mistaken regarding completeObs. My (very short) testing suggests that completeObs=TRUE means impute the missing values through iterative PCA and return the full data with missing values imputed. See
?pca
...
completeObs: Sets the ‘completeObs’ slot on the resulting ‘pcaRes’
          object containing the original data with but with all NAs
          replaced with the estimates.

So, for example:

d <- data.frame(a=runif(10), b=runif(10), c=runif(10), foo=letters[round(runif(10, 1, 3))], bar=runif(10))

# add an NA
d[1,2] <- NA

library("pcaMethods")
library("autoplot")

# do not complete obs
pca <- pca(d[1:3], mode="svd", completeObs=F)
# pca@completeObs is NULL so
head(fortify(pca, type="obs"), 3)
# does not return any data, only the PCs and associated quantities
# but one can still supply the data to have it cbinded with those quantities
head(fortify(pca, type="obs", data=d), 3)

# now, complete obs
pca <- pca(d[1:3], mode="svd", completeObs=T)
# now pca@completeObs contains the imputed data
pca@completeObs
# and we use that in fortify
head(fortify(pca, type="obs"), 3)
# supplying the data replaces it
head(fortify(pca, type="obs", data=d), 3)

The behaviour I want to change is the last one: instead of replacing the data that comes from the PCA (the one with missing values filled) fortify should just supplement it with the additional columns foo and bar. This way, all possibilities would be covered (if you really want the data with NAs just use completeObs=FALSE).

One thing I am not sure about is how pca() treats missing values when completeObs=FALSE. It seems to me that it still does the imputation and computes the pca on the complete data afterwards, because it still outputs PCs for the lines with NAs and they as the same as when completeObs=TRUE, only,  it does not return the imputed data.
I guess if the user really wants the NAs removed, he can always use na.omit() on the data fed to pca() but the choice of automatically imputing data is a surprising one, since you usually want the functions to let you know that there were NAs when they are there. An explicit option might be preferable.

As a side note: the code for pca() shows that when method=svd and that there are missing values, the method is switched to nipals automatically, without informing the user. A warning() or a message() would be in order I would think.

Okay, to expand on this, having looked in guides via joran on SO.

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg, colour=factor(cyl))) + geom_line()
p + opts(legend.title=theme_text(size = 15))
# great that bumped the font size up, the 'original/old way'

# now use the new guides options
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(title.theme = theme_text(size = 8)))
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(title.theme = theme_text(size = 8), title.position="left"))
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(title.theme = theme_text(size = 8), title.position="left", title.vjust=2))
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(title.theme = theme_text(size = 8), title.position="left", title.vjust=2, title.hjust=1))
# so we can change the font size, move it to one size, change vertical alignment but not horiztonal?

# but what if it's on top?
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(title.theme = theme_text(size = 8)))
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(title.theme = theme_text(size = 8), title.hjust=1))
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(title.theme = theme_text(size = 8), title.hjust=1, title.vjust=2))
# can change size but not alignment

# what about nrow
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow=2,title.theme = theme_text(size = 8)))
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow=2,title.theme = theme_text(size = 8), title.hjust=1))
p + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow=2,title.theme = theme_text(size = 8), title.hjust=1, title.vjust=2))
# so when it's on top we can adjust the horizontal but not the vertical alignment

>From this I conclude that we can't tweak vjust when the title is on top, can't tweak hjust when it's the on the side and can only tweak hjust on the top when it's forced wider with nrow. To me this isn't optimal functionality and is more restrictive than what we used to have? Or is there something I'm missing.

The way I came across this was through tweaking a graph for publication, in a tight space (2.6" wide output), and needing to move the legend title just a fraction. I wrote the theme for this particular graph I'm doing a few months ago, then noticed it wasn't doing now what it did then, then noticed the move to 'guides' via joran @SO, then wound up here(/ in this position).

Cheers

Hi everyone -

I've updated vtest to be able to save R graphical output from anything (including base and grid graphics), not just ggplot2.

Here is an example test script that would go in a package's visual_test/ directory. I've put the output here:
http://stdout.org/~winston/vtest-expression/html/expression_examples.html
==================================
vcontext("expression_examples")

# Works with base graphics
save_vtest2("base graphics", {
  plot(1:10, (1:10)^2)
})

# Works with grid
library(grid)
save_vtest2("grid graphics", {
  grid.newpage()
  grid.draw(rectGrob(width=unit(1,"cm"), height=unit(1,"cm")))
})

# Works with ggplot objects
save_vtest2("ggplot2 graphics", {
  ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point()
})

# Can find vars in parent environment
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg))
save_vtest2("ggplot2 graphics - vars in parent", {
  p + geom_point()
})

end_vcontext()
===================================

Code is here:
https://github.com/wch/vtest

-Winston

Hi everyone -

We have a release candidate for ggplot2 0.9.2. It will be in the RC
phase for a month (hopefully) before it is sent to CRAN.

It would be very helpful if you could try out the RC version and see
if it breaks any of your existing code. To install the new version to
a development library directory (~/R-dev):
  install.packages("devtools")
  library(devtools)
  dev_mode()
  install_github("gtable", branch = "gtable-0.1.1-rc")
  install_github("scales", branch = "scales-0.2.2-rc")
  install_github("ggplot2", branch = "ggplot2-0.9.2-rc")

Once it is installed, you can try out your existing code that uses ggplot2.

You are likely to encounter messages about deprecated functions:
opts(), and theme_text(), theme_rect(), and theme_line(), but existing
code should continue to work. Here's a summary of the changes:

* opts() is deprecated. It is replaced with theme().
* theme_text(), theme_rect(), theme_line() are deprecated. You can
replace them with element_text(), element_rect(), and element_line().
* theme_segment() is deprecated. Its functionality is now handled by
element_line().
* The previous way to set the title of a plot was opts(title="Title
text"). Instead, use ggtitle("Title text") or labs(title="Title
text").

There are also a number of enhancements to the theming system. If
you'd like to read more about it, see:
  https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/New-theme-system

For the full list of changes to this version of ggplot2, see:
  https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/master/NEWS

If you encounter any problems with the new version, please post to
this list, or file an issue on Github.

Thanks!
-Winston
